title: U.S. Senate (special) · Florida

context.text: Special election to fill the remainder of the term Marco Rubio (R) was elected to in 2022, which expires in January 2029. Rubio resigned on January 20, 2025 after being confirmed as U.S. Secretary of State; Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) appointed Ashley Moody as his interim successor the next day. In the August 18, 2026 primaries, Moody defeated Chris Gleason, Ernie Rivera and Neelam Perry for the Republican nomination (79.6%), and Angela Nixon defeated Alex Vindman for the Democratic nomination (55.9%-44.1%).

candidates.name: Ashley Moody
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 18, 2026 Republican primary with 79.6% of the vote.
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Senator from Florida (appointed January 2025; assumed office 2025)

summary.text: Ashley Moody is the incumbent Republican U.S. Senator from Florida. A Plant City native and University of Florida graduate, she worked as a lawyer and federal prosecutor, served as a Hillsborough County circuit judge, and was elected Florida Attorney General in 2018 and 2022 before Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Senate in January 2025. She is running to serve the remainder of Marco Rubio's term, which expires in January 2029.

background.text: Born in Plant City, Florida, in 1975; her Senate biography describes her as a fifth-generation Floridian.
Earned bachelor's and master's degrees in accounting (1993, 1996) and a J.D. (2000) from the University of Florida, and an LL.M. in international law from Stetson University College of Law (2010).

Began her legal career at the law firm Holland & Knight, practicing commercial litigation, then served as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Middle District of Florida, prosecuting drug, firearm and fraud offenses; she was also an adjunct professor at Stetson University College of Law.

Elected in 2006 to the Thirteenth Judicial Circuit Court in Hillsborough County at age 31, which her Senate biography describes as making her the youngest judge in Florida; she served on the bench from 2007 to 2017.
Won the 2018 election for Florida Attorney General (52.1% to 46.1% over Sean Shaw) and was re-elected in 2022 (60.6% to 39.4% over Aramis Ayala); she served from 2019 to 2025.

As Attorney General, she served on the Presidential Commission on Law Enforcement and the Administration of Justice during the first Trump administration and chaired Florida's Statewide Council on Human Trafficking, according to her Senate biography, which also cites the state's share of opioid litigation settlements.
Appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to succeed Marco Rubio after he became Secretary of State, and sworn into the U.S. Senate on January 21, 2025.

Serves on the Judiciary, Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committees, the Special Committee on Aging, and the Joint Economic Committee. Her Senate biography says she and her husband, Justin, a career law enforcement officer, have two sons.

priorities.text: Says she is a supporter of President Trump's agenda and is 'dedicated to America First policies that promote law and order, economic prosperity, and American sovereignty.'
Campaigns on her record as Attorney General, citing efforts to 'enhance public safety, strengthen law enforcement, and crack down on violent crime.'
Describes herself as a national leader on 'protecting religious freedom and the sanctity of life.'

positions.summary: Is a cosponsor of the Constitutional Concealed Carry Reciprocity Act, which would let people with a concealed-carry privilege in their home state carry in other states that allow concealed carry.
positions.quote: I’m proud to cosponsor the Constitutional Concealed Carry Reciprocity Act

positions.summary: Introduced the Child Interstate Abortion Notification Act in January 2026, which would make it a federal offense to knowingly transport a minor across state lines without complying with parental consent and notification laws for abortion.
positions.quote: I’m introducing the Child Interstate Abortion Notification Act to strengthen protections for parents and families by ensuring compliance with state parental notification and consent laws.

positions.summary: Is a cosponsor of the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025, which would generally bar transgender girls and women from school athletic programs for women and girls.
positions.quote: Male athletes have no business competing in women's sports

candidates.name: Angela Nixon
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 18, 2026 Democratic primary over Alex Vindman, 55.9%-44.1%.

summary.text: Angela (Angie) Nixon is the Democratic nominee. A Jacksonville native, she has served in the Florida House of Representatives since 2020, and has worked as a union organizer, executive director of the coalition Florida for All, and a small-business and bookstore owner. She says she is running on lowering costs, health care, affordable child care and protecting Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid.

background.text: Born February 27, 1984, in Jacksonville, Florida, and raised in the city's Moncrief neighborhood by a single mother who worked two jobs, according to Wikipedia; her campaign website also describes her upbringing in a predominantly Black Jacksonville neighborhood.
Earned a B.A. in political science from the University of Florida in 2007.
Ran unsuccessfully for the Jacksonville City Council in 2008, then worked as an aide to state Rep. Mia Jones, according to Wikipedia.

Has worked as a union organizer, including as a higher education director for the Florida Public Service Union and earlier as state field director for SEIU, per Wikipedia and Ballotpedia; she has led the statewide coalition Florida for All since 2022.

Co-founded the Melanin Market, an outdoor market for small food businesses, and in 2024 opened Cafe Resistance, a bookstore and coffee shop in Jacksonville that serves as a community space, according to Wikipedia; her campaign website says she runs a bookstore and community hub.

Won the 2020 Democratic primary for Florida House District 14, defeating incumbent Kimberly Daniels, 59.8% to 40.2%, and took office that November; after redistricting she was elected in 2022 in District 13.

In the Florida House she has worked on legislation expanding child care access and addressing grocery price-gouging, and describes herself as having led opposition to the state's voting maps, according to her campaign website and Ballotpedia survey.
Launched her U.S. Senate campaign in January 2026 and won the August 18 Democratic primary.

priorities.text: Lowering everyday costs amid what she calls an affordability crisis, including housing and insurance costs.
priorities.quote: Floridians are being crushed by an affordability crisis created by greed and corruption.

priorities.text: Creating a healthcare system that works for everyone and protecting Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and the VA.

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page calls for Medicare for All covering every person in America.
positions.quote: Medicare for All that covers every person in America — free at the point of service, with no premiums, no deductibles, no copays, and no surprise bills.

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page calls for universal, high-quality child care and pre-kindergarten for every family regardless of income.
positions.quote: Universal, high-quality child care and pre-kindergarten for every family, regardless of income

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page lists protecting reproductive freedom, including the right to abortion.
positions.quote: the right to abortion, contraception, and IVF, free from political interference

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page calls for abolishing ICE, a moratorium on deportations pending an audit of enforcement practices, and ending mass deportation.
positions.quote: mass incarceration and mass deportation are moral failures, and I will fight in the United States Senate to end them.

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page calls for a 5% annual wealth tax on billionaires and for closing corporate tax loopholes.
positions.quote: A 5% annual wealth tax on billionaires.

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page calls for a union-built transition to renewable energy and for ending taxpayer subsidies for fossil fuel corporations.
positions.quote: A bold, union-built transition to renewable energy

positions.summary: Her campaign priorities page calls for raising the federal minimum wage to a living wage indexed to inflation.
positions.quote: Raising the federal minimum wage to a real living wage, indexed to inflation

record.text: As a Florida state representative, worked on legislation expanding childcare access and addressing price-gouging.

candidates.name: Neil Gillespie

summary.text: Neil Gillespie is a no-party-affiliation candidate who describes himself as the founder and director of Justice Network, an advocacy and news organization. He says he is running because of what he calls a lack of due process in state and federal courts, and on separation of powers and health care reform.

background.text: According to his Ballotpedia survey response, he moved to Florida from Pennsylvania in 1993, where he had been a licensed motor vehicle dealer.
Earned an associate degree from the Wharton School's evening division at the University of Pennsylvania (1988) and a bachelor's degree from The Evergreen State College (1995).
Describes himself as founder and director of Justice Network, an organization engaged in advocacy, education and news gathering to help people fight injustice.

priorities.text: Lists restoring checks and balances and the separation of powers as the first of three key campaign messages.
priorities.quote: Restore checks and balances in government, separation of powers.

priorities.text: Lists health care reform as a key campaign message, proposing national coverage with an opt-out.
priorities.quote: I propose national health coverage, with the ability to opt-out.

priorities.text: Lists the safety of Jews in the United States as a key campaign message.
priorities.quote: Guarantee the safety of Jews in the United States.

positions.summary: Proposes national health coverage with the ability to opt out.
positions.quote: I propose national health coverage, with the ability to opt-out.

positions.summary: Supports lawful removal of people who entered illegally and a path to citizenship for immigrants who follow the rules; opposes what he calls the spectacle of activists confronting ICE.
positions.quote: I support the lawful removal of people who enter the United States illegally, but not the spectacle created by activists confronting ICE.

candidates.researchNotes: Source: his 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey (also reproduced on his campaign blog). Scribd press release could not be read. No stance found on other guide issues.
